label: copy-phase input token o (fed-back o)
explanation: Fires when the letter o is fed back as an input during the copy phase (t > L). Essentially 100% of activation mass is on copy-phase o inputs; it never fires on o (or anything else) during the original phase or on <DEL>, and the ~56 off-token activations are tiny. Magnitude is largest early in the copy (o fed back at recall_idx 1-2, i.e. o was one of the first two original tokens; top examples ~0.9-1.0 of max) and weaker for o later in the copy (~0.05-0.3). About 27% of copy-phase o inputs stay inactive, mostly in short sequences (L=3-4) or at the final copy step; adding L>=5 or to_go>=1 gives only small F1 gains (0.84 -> 0.86).

issues: The core claims hold. Activation is 0 in the original phase and on <DEL>; the copy phase carries 100% of the mass. in_tok=o holds 66353 of 66409 active dev steps. The 45 test misses outside the predicate carry 0.0% of the mass. Most of them are the step just before o is fed back, where o is the output (e.g. 'f o x ... <DEL> [f:0.09] o'), and they are tiny.

The account of the 27% inactive copy-phase o inputs is partly wrong. Inactivity is not mostly L=3-4 or the final step. Precision falls steadily with outputs remaining (to_go=7: 1.00, 5: 1.00, 4: 0.93, 3: 0.82, 2: 0.71, 1: 0.59, 0: 0.40). It also depends on L. By L and recall_idx: L=9 is r1-3 = 1.00, r4 0.76, r5 0.61, r6 0.69, r8 (final step) 0.81. L=7 is r4 0.74, r5 0.46, r6 0.33. L=5 is r1 0.73, r2 0.97, r4 0.37. L=3 is r1 0.09, r2 0.00. So many inactive steps sit in the middle-to-late copy positions at every length, and the final step in L=9 is usually active.

I found no token or history factor behind the mid-position inactivity. A second o in the copy, in_count>=2, digit count, a digit or vowel as the previous token, and next_out all leave precision around 0.57-0.64. It looks like a graded fall in magnitude by position that crosses the activity threshold, not a separate class.
A position-aware predicate gains only a little on test: F1 0.865 against 0.845 for the original. That fits the original agent's choice to keep the simple predicate.
